cards.front: In male reproductive-tract development, what happens when one link in the chain (a cell, hormone, enzyme or receptor) is lost completely and early?
cards.back: Everything downstream of that link fails, while the other developmental branches carry on.
cards.quote: Break one link and everything downstream of it fails, while the other developmental branches carry on.

cards.front: Every embryo starts with a {{c1::bipotential}} gonad, one that can develop into either a testis or an ovary.
cards.quote: Every embryo starts with a bipotential gonad, one that can develop into either a testis or an ovary.
cards.section: Making a testis: SRY flips the supporting cells

cards.front: In most mammals, how does the Y-linked gene SRY start testis determination?
cards.back: It raises SOX9, a transcription factor, in the gonad's supporting-cell precursors, which then become Sertoli cells.
cards.quote: the Y-linked gene SRY starts testis determination by raising SOX9, a transcription factor, in the gonad's supporting-cell precursors, which then become Sertoli cells
cards.section: Making a testis: SRY flips the supporting cells

cards.front: Is the ovary simply the default gonad that forms when SRY is missing?
cards.back: No. The ovary has its own gene program that pushes the other way, and the testis and ovary programs compete in the same supporting cells.
cards.quote: The ovary is not what is left when SRY is missing: it has its own gene program that pushes the other way
cards.section: Making a testis: SRY flips the supporting cells

cards.front: An XY mouse embryo lacks a working Sry gene; the rest of its genome is normal. Predict the gonad, AMH, testosterone and DHT outcomes.
cards.back: No testis forms: the supporting cells follow the ovarian program. No AMH, no Leydig testosterone, no DHT.
cards.why: SRY is the first link, so every downstream link fails: gonad, ducts and outside all change.
cards.quote: SRY is the first link, so everything downstream fails: no AMH, no Leydig testosterone, no DHT.
cards.section: Making a testis: SRY flips the supporting cells

cards.front: What can the Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts become?
cards.back: The epididymis, the vas deferens and the seminal vesicles.
cards.quote: The Wolffian ducts (also called mesonephric ducts) can become the epididymis, where sperm mature after leaving the testis, the vas deferens
cards.section: Two ducts, two jobs, two signals

cards.front: What can the Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts become?
cards.back: The oviducts, the uterus and the upper vagina.
cards.quote: The Müllerian ducts (paramesonephric ducts) can become the oviducts, the uterus and the upper vagina.
cards.section: Two ducts, two jobs, two signals

cards.front: Jost removed the testes from XY rabbit fetuses early, before the ducts had changed. What did the animals develop, and what does it show?
cards.back: They kept the Müllerian ducts and lost most Wolffian ducts: a female-typical tract. The male-typical tract needs the testis.
cards.quote: It keeps its Müllerian ducts and loses most of its Wolffian ducts, so it develops a female-typical tract.
cards.section: Two ducts, two jobs, two signals

cards.front: Jost also removed the ovaries from XX rabbit fetuses. What happened to the tract, and what does it show?
cards.back: The tract was still female-typical. The female-typical tract does not need an ovarian secretion.
cards.why: This concerns the tract only; the ovary itself is built by an active program.
cards.quote: So the female-typical tract does not need an ovarian secretion; the male-typical tract needs the testis.
cards.section: Two ducts, two jobs, two signals

cards.front: Jost removed the testes of XY rabbit fetuses and gave testosterone instead. Which ducts were kept, and what did he infer?
cards.back: Both pairs: Wolffian ducts were rescued, but Müllerian ducts stayed. Testosterone cannot remove the Müllerian ducts, so the testis must make a second signal, a Müllerian inhibitor.
cards.quote: It rescued one pair but could not remove the other, so he inferred a second signal, a Müllerian inhibitor.
cards.section: Two ducts, two jobs, two signals

cards.front: Which testis cell makes anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), and what is its target response?
cards.back: The Sertoli cell; AMH makes the Müllerian ducts regress.
cards.quote: Sertoli cell → AMH → Müllerian ducts regress.
cards.section: Two ducts, two jobs, two signals

cards.front: Which testis cell makes testosterone in the human fetus, where is it, and what does testosterone do to the ducts?
cards.back: The Leydig cell, a steroid-making cell between the developing tubules; testosterone keeps the Wolffian ducts.
cards.quote: the Leydig cell, a steroid-making cell between the developing tubules
cards.section: Two ducts, two jobs, two signals

cards.front: Male mice lack only the AMH gene; their testes form. Predict their ducts and whether they make sperm.
cards.back: They keep a uterus and oviducts and also keep Wolffian derivatives; their testes make functional sperm. Most are infertile because the retained organs hinder sperm transfer.
cards.why: One broken link (AMH) changes one branch; the testosterone branch carries on.
cards.quote: They keep a uterus and oviducts, because nothing removes the Müllerian ducts, and they keep their male (Wolffian) derivatives, because testosterone is still made.
cards.section: Two ducts, two jobs, two signals

cards.front: What does the AMH-null male mouse experiment establish, and what does it not establish?
cards.back: It shows AMH is necessary for Müllerian regression in mice. It does not locate AMH's receptor or measure a human response curve.
cards.quote: The experiment shows that AMH is necessary for Müllerian regression in mice; it does not locate AMH's receptor or measure a human response curve.
cards.section: Two ducts, two jobs, two signals

cards.front: The enzyme {{c1::5-alpha-reductase type 2}}, encoded by the gene SRD5A2, converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
cards.quote: The enzyme 5-alpha-reductase type 2, encoded by the gene SRD5A2, converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
cards.section: The outside needs DHT (in humans)

cards.front: In the human fetus, what is DHT signalling needed for?
cards.back: Full masculinization of the external genitalia; it also supports prostate development.
cards.quote: Human fetal DHT signalling is needed for full masculinization of the external genitalia and supports prostate development.
cards.section: The outside needs DHT (in humans)

cards.front: Testosterone and DHT act through the same androgen receptor. Why do tissues convert testosterone to DHT at all?
cards.back: DHT holds the receptor more tightly, so tissues that make DHT amplify the androgen signal.
cards.quote: DHT holds the receptor more tightly, so tissues that make DHT amplify the signal.
cards.section: The outside needs DHT (in humans)

cards.front: In humans, the genital tubercle contributes to the glans penis or clitoris, and the {{c1::labioscrotal swellings}} become the scrotum or the labia majora.
cards.quote: the labioscrotal swellings become the scrotum or the labia majora
cards.section: The outside needs DHT (in humans)

cards.front: An XY embryo has normal testes and normal AMH, but its androgen receptor does not work at all. Predict the Müllerian ducts, the Wolffian ducts and the external genitalia.
cards.back: Müllerian ducts regress; Wolffian ducts are not kept; the outside is female-typical.
cards.why: AMH does not act through AR, but both androgen branches (testosterone and DHT) run through AR.
cards.quote: AMH does not act through the androgen receptor, so the Müllerian ducts should still regress.
cards.section: The outside needs DHT (in humans)

cards.front: A human XY fetus has normal testes but no working SRD5A2. Predict the Müllerian ducts, the Wolffian derivatives and the external genitalia.
cards.back: Müllerian ducts usually absent; Wolffian derivatives generally kept; external genitalia less masculinized.
cards.why: AMH is intact and testosterone still acts on AR; only the DHT branch is missing.
cards.quote: Testosterone still acts on AR, so the Wolffian derivatives are generally kept. Only DHT is missing, so the outside is less masculinized.
cards.section: The outside needs DHT (in humans)

cards.front: In 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency, why do the external genitalia partly masculinize at puberty?
cards.back: The high testosterone of puberty can partly substitute, so the DHT branch is a matter of potency, not an absolute switch.
cards.quote: the high testosterone of puberty partly masculinizes the external genitalia, so the DHT branch is a matter of potency, not an absolute switch
cards.section: When a link is only partly broken

cards.front: How is the fetal steroid step in the mouse testis different from the human picture of "Leydig testosterone"?
cards.back: Fetal mouse Leydig cells make mostly androstenedione, and fetal Sertoli cells convert it to testosterone, so the link is split between two cell types.
cards.quote: In the fetal mouse, Leydig cells make mostly androstenedione, and fetal Sertoli cells convert it to testosterone
cards.section: Mouse versus human steroid steps

cards.front: In the adult testis, which cell makes testosterone, where is it, and which pituitary hormone drives it?
cards.back: Leydig cells, outside the tubules in the interstitium, under luteinizing hormone (LH).
cards.quote: Outside the tubules: Leydig cells make testosterone under the pituitary hormone luteinizing hormone (LH).
cards.section: The adult testis: the same two cells, two compartments

cards.front: In the adult testis, what do Sertoli cells do and what signals do they respond to?
cards.back: Inside the tubules they nourish the germ cells; they respond to FSH and to local testosterone.
cards.quote: Inside the tubules: Sertoli cells nourish the germ cells.
cards.section: The adult testis: the same two cells, two compartments

cards.front: Why is testosterone inside the testis far higher than testosterone in the blood?
cards.back: Leydig cells sit next to the tubules and their testosterone reaches them directly, so intratesticular testosterone is far higher than circulating testosterone.
cards.quote: Leydig testosterone reaches the tubules directly, so intratesticular testosterone is far higher than circulating testosterone.
cards.section: The adult testis: the same two cells, two compartments

cards.front: What forms the blood-testis barrier?
cards.back: A junctional seal between neighbouring Sertoli cells inside each tubule, not capillary endothelium.
cards.quote: the blood-testis barrier is a junctional seal between neighbouring Sertoli cells, not capillary endothelium
cards.section: The adult testis: the same two cells, two compartments

cards.front: Which germ cells lie in the basal compartment and which in the adluminal compartment of the seminiferous tubule?
cards.back: Basal: spermatogonia and early spermatocytes. Adluminal (toward the lumen): later meiotic cells and spermatids.
cards.quote: an adluminal compartment, toward the lumen, which holds later meiotic cells and spermatids (haploid products of meiosis)
cards.section: The adult testis: the same two cells, two compartments

cards.front: How do testosterone and inhibin B feed back on pituitary gonadotropins?
cards.back: Testosterone restrains LH and FSH output, partly after conversion to estradiol. Sertoli inhibin B selectively inhibits FSH.
cards.quote: Sertoli cells make inhibin B, which selectively inhibits FSH
cards.section: The adult testis: the same two cells, two compartments

cards.front: In an adult feedback model, inhibin B falls while GnRH input, sex-steroid feedback and pituitary sensitivity are held constant. Predict FSH and LH.
cards.back: FSH rises; LH stays unchanged.
cards.why: Inhibin B selectively inhibits FSH, so removing it releases only FSH.
cards.quote: Sertoli cells make inhibin B, which selectively inhibits FSH
cards.section: The adult testis: the same two cells, two compartments

cards.front: A man injects testosterone and his blood testosterone rises. Predict his LH and FSH, his intratesticular testosterone and his sperm production.
cards.back: LH and FSH fall; intratesticular testosterone falls steeply while blood testosterone is high; sperm production usually falls (it can be suppressed, sometimes to infertility).
cards.why: Negative feedback cuts LH, so Leydig cells make little testosterone; germ cells lose local androgen and FSH support.
cards.quote: testosterone inside the testis falls steeply while blood testosterone is high
cards.section: The adult testis: the same two cells, two compartments

cards.front: Healthy men received testosterone injections for three weeks, with or without low-dose hCG. What happened to intratesticular testosterone, and why did hCG matter?
cards.back: With placebo, LH and FSH were suppressed and intratesticular testosterone fell by about 94%. With hCG, which acts on the LH receptor, it stayed in the normal range.
cards.quote: Men who also received low-dose hCG, which acts on the LH receptor, kept intratesticular testosterone in the normal range.
cards.section: The testosterone-injection trial

cards.front: Mice lacking androgen receptor only in Sertoli cells have spermatocytes that synapse and recombine chromosomes but fail to acquire competence for meiotic division. What does this suggest?
cards.back: A somatic (Sertoli-mediated) androgen response supports later meiotic competence; it does not imply every early meiotic event needs androgen.
cards.quote: That supports a Sertoli-mediated requirement without implying that every early meiotic event requires androgen
cards.section: Sertoli androgen receptor deletions

cards.front: In human spermatogenesis, what is the conventional length of one epithelial cycle, and about how long does one batch take from differentiating spermatogonium to spermiation?
cards.back: About 16 days per cycle; about 74 days in total (textbook human values).
cards.quote: Any one batch needs about 74 days, the textbook human total from a differentiating spermatogonium to spermiation, to finish.
cards.section: A sperm ejaculated today began developing about two and a half months ago

cards.front: Human spermatogenesis takes about 74 days and the epithelial cycle is 16 days. Assuming steady production and constant cycle length, how many cycles does one lineage span, and about how many months is that?
cards.back: 74 / 16 = 4.625, about 4.6 cycles; 74 days is about 2.4 months. Adding epididymal transit, an ejaculated sperm began developing about two and a half months earlier.
cards.quote: Cycles per lineage = 74 days / 16 days per cycle = 4.625, about 4.6 cycles.
cards.section: A sperm ejaculated today began developing about two and a half months ago

cards.front: Why do some books give 64 days instead of 74 days for human spermatogenesis?
cards.back: They leave out the early spermatogonial divisions, so check which starting cell a number uses.
cards.quote: Some books give 64 days because they leave out the early spermatogonial divisions
cards.section: A sperm ejaculated today began developing about two and a half months ago

cards.front: A made-up tracer model assumes a 16-day epithelial cycle, 3.5 cycles remaining from the labelled stage to spermiation, and 10 days of epididymal transit with no storage delay. What label-to-ejaculate lag does it predict?
cards.back: 3.5 × 16 = 56 days in the testis; 56 + 10 = 66 days.
cards.why: Count the cycles left from the labelled stage, multiply by 16 days, then add transit.
cards.quote: Predicted label-to-ejaculate lag = 56 days + 10 days = 66 days.
cards.section: Timing: 64 versus 74 days, and the tracer lag

cards.front: A deuterium study measured a label-to-ejaculate lag of 64 ± 8 days (mean ± SD). A model predicts 66 days. Is the prediction inside mean ± 1 SD, and does that validate the model's assumed cycles and transit time?
cards.back: Yes: 64 − 8 = 56 to 64 + 8 = 72 days, which contains 66. No: different component delays could give the same total.
cards.quote: different component delays could give the same total
cards.section: Timing: 64 versus 74 days, and the tracer lag

cards.front: A man has a high fever that harms developing germ cells for a few days. When should a change in his semen be expected to appear?
cards.back: Weeks to months later, up to about two to three months, because sperm in today's ejaculate began developing about two and a half months earlier.
cards.why: Rests on the 74-day spermatogenesis plus epididymal transit.
cards.quote: Anything that changes sperm production, such as a drug, a fever or the testosterone injections above, shows up in semen weeks to months later.
cards.section: A sperm ejaculated today began developing about two and a half months ago

cards.front: Trace the signalling pathway from nitric oxide to relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle during erection.
cards.back: NO activates guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP; protein kinase G links cGMP to lower cytosolic calcium and smooth-muscle relaxation.
cards.quote: NO activates guanylyl cyclase, raising cyclic GMP (cGMP), and protein kinase G links cGMP to lower cytosolic calcium and smooth-muscle relaxation.
cards.section: Erection and ejaculation: three phases, three outflows

cards.front: Why do PDE5 inhibitors support erection?
cards.back: PDE5 breaks down cGMP, so blocking it keeps cGMP high and favours smooth-muscle relaxation.
cards.quote: PDE5 breaks down cGMP, so PDE5 inhibitors keep cGMP high
cards.section: Erection and ejaculation: three phases, three outflows

cards.front: Electrical stimulation of isolated rabbit corpus cavernosum raises endogenous NO production, with downstream signalling intact and cGMP breakdown unchanged. Predict cGMP, cytosolic calcium and tension.
cards.back: cGMP rises, cytosolic calcium falls, tension falls.
cards.why: NO activates guanylyl cyclase; protein kinase G links cGMP to lower calcium and relaxation.
cards.quote: NO activates guanylyl cyclase, raising cyclic GMP (cGMP)
cards.section: Erection and ejaculation: three phases, three outflows

cards.front: How does relaxation of cavernosal and arterial smooth muscle produce a rigid erection?
cards.back: Inflow rises and the sinusoids fill, compressing the veins beneath the tunica, so venous drainage is restricted.
cards.quote: When it and the arterial smooth muscle relax, the tissue fills and compresses the veins beneath the tunica, its fibrous covering.
cards.section: Erection and ejaculation: three phases, three outflows

cards.front: Assign each phase to its main outflow: erection, emission, expulsion.
cards.back: Erection: pelvic parasympathetic (nitrergic) pathways. Emission: sympathetic. Expulsion: somatic pudendal motor output.
cards.quote: Expulsion is the rhythmic outward movement driven by somatic pudendal motor output to muscles including bulbospongiosus.
cards.section: Erection and ejaculation: three phases, three outflows

cards.front: A man takes an alpha-adrenergic blocker. Predict the effect on emission and on erection.
cards.back: Emission can be impaired; erection is largely preserved.
cards.why: Emission is mainly sympathetic; erection depends mainly on parasympathetic and nitrergic pathways. Separate outflows fail separately.
cards.quote: sympathetic nerve damage or an alpha-blocker can impair emission, while erection, which depends mainly on parasympathetic and nitrergic pathways, is largely preserved
cards.section: Erection and ejaculation: three phases, three outflows

cards.front: A colleague claims testosterone alone gives an XY embryo a male-typical tract. Design fetal rabbit or mouse experiments that test the claim.
cards.back: Remove XY rabbit fetal testes early and give testosterone: both duct pairs stay, so the claim fails. In mice, delete AMH or its receptor (Müllerian ducts persist) and delete AR (Müllerian ducts regress, Wolffian ducts lost).
cards.why: Controls: littermates, confirmed deletions, matched ages inside the duct-response window.
cards.quote: Together they show two signals with separate targets.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Mice lacking Sertoli-cell AR from fetal life make almost no spermatids. How would you test whether this reflects failed Sertoli maturation or an ongoing adult requirement?
cards.back: Delete AR only in adult Sertoli cells using a conditional (Cre-targeted) allele, verify loss, include no-Cre and delivery controls, and follow a time series. Adult requirement predicts meiotic arrest and eventual loss of epididymal sperm.
cards.quote: If adult signalling is required, predict meiotic arrest and eventual depletion of epididymal sperm.
cards.section: Sertoli androgen receptor deletions

cards.front: In scrotal mammals, the testis is cooler than the core, with countercurrent heat exchange between incoming arterial blood and the surrounding {{c1::pampiniform plexus}}, a network of testicular veins.
cards.quote: countercurrent heat exchange between incoming arterial blood and the surrounding pampiniform plexus, a network of testicular veins
cards.section: Two vascular details

cards.front: In an adult, AR-mediated feedback is lost. Using the feedback loop, predict the direction of LH drive, and say whether blood testosterone can be predicted with certainty.
cards.back: LH drive should rise because AR-mediated feedback is lost. Testosterone cannot be predicted with certainty: it depends on species and testis function.
cards.why: Rests on testosterone restraining LH output; normal or high testosterone is a human AR-loss pattern, not a guaranteed value.
cards.quote: Loss of AR-mediated feedback predicts increased LH drive, but testosterone concentrations depend on species and testis function
cards.section: LH and testosterone after receptor loss
